Q: Is it fine to use IQueryable in BLL? A:

If you are using EF you don't mock the DAL! Use an In-Memory version of the database and then seed it with the data you need for testing. So yes, if you want to mock the DAL, repo pattern might simplify that process, but in EF with IQueryable, we use different patterns to test. You need to adapt your thinking to a different process, not just your code.

Q: Mtime.Span.pp vs Timedesc.pp A:

The function Mtime.pp is Format.formatter -> Mtime.span -> unit and it doesn't seem to accept the formatter as its first parameter. I thought I can format the datetime.

First of all, I think you mean "format string". That function does take a formatter as its first parameter.

Mtime doesn't give you a datetime. As the docs say

Timestamps represent system-relative monotonic timestamps, their absolute value is meaningless but they can be compared across the processes of an operating system run.

So they don't take a formatter because they don't have enough info for that to be useful.

Timedesc.pp expects unit as the 1st parameter. What is the purpose of that ?

That's not the first argument, it's the second:

val pp : ?format:string -> unit -> Stdlib.Format.formatter -> t -> unit

The first argument is an optional format string. Optional arguments aren't erased until a positional argument is supplied. The unit is only there to allow you to erase the optional argument - that is, Timedesc.pp () has the right type for a pretty printer. If you didn't have the unit, you would have to write either Timedesc.pp ?format:None or fun fmtr -> Timedesc.pp fmtr in order to get something with the right type for a pretty printer without supplying a format string.

Q: How to declare a variable using std::meta::info of a non static data member inside a template for loop? A:

In this loop:

template for (constexpr std::meta::info MemberInfo : /* non-static data members */) {
    using MemberType = [:MemberInfo:];

MemberInfo is a reflection which represents a non-static data member - it can only be spliced in certain contexts. Like obj.[:MemberInfo:] or &[:MemberInfo:]. It does not represent a type, which is what you need on the right-hand side of an alias declaration.

Hopefully a production implementation will provide a clear error message in this context, since it certainly can, but the one you're using is an experimental one. That will all get better over time.

What you need is a type — specifically a reflection representing a type. That is:

    using MemberType = [: type_of(MemberInfo) :];
    //                    ^~~~~~~

With that change, your code compiles.

Conceptually, you can think of this as the category error of writing this:

using MemberType = Position::X; // error: not a type

instead of this:

using MemberType = decltype(Position::X); // ok

Q: Sort a column of data to align cells with a separate "key" column? A:

XLOOKUP() would be more simpler. Try-

=XLOOKUP(D2,B:B,B:B,"")

Q: C Syntax Parsing Only A:

This is an XY problem. What are you really trying to do? What is the original and underlying problem that you need to solve? What is the parsing supposed to do for you, and how will it solve that original problem?

With that said, almost every parser-generator tool have a C syntax file readily available. And the core of C is relatively straightforward making it not too hard to create a parser for it. Granted, I have a bit of experience, but I could do a hand-crafted lexer and parser in a work day. Maybe two, to handle the tricky edge-cases and added unit testing.

Q: How do you make a default constructor and fix the type deduction error indicated by E3158 and E0289? A:

I am making several template classes and just realized that their non-initialized declarations give errors E3158 and E0289: indicating that my compiler cannot identify the class's template arguments.

test is the name of a class template and as such it need a template argument T for the template parameter arb so that test<T> becomes a class type.

The difference is important. Class-types can have an instance of that class-type but class templates can't have an instance as they're not a type!

There's no way for the compiler to infer the type of arb by itself.

I am wondering whether there is any way around this? Can I maybe force the default constructor to pick a type?

You can use a default argument for the template parameter arb if you think it should be used when no type for arb is specified as in:

//-----------------------vvv--->specify the default type here
template <typename arb = int>
class test{//...};
test t{}; //now this will work

Q: How to resolve Snyk Path Traversal Warning? A:

Adding this line will appease the Snyk scanner:

filename = filename.replace('..', '')

Snyk is pretty stupid on this one; it doesn't recognize more complex sanitation techniques that encompass removing traversal techniques.
